main.text: It is proved that פרס peres is the ossifrage.

In the list of unclean birds פרס peres is second in order. The Greeks render it τὸν γρύπα [ton grypa]. Hence Jerome, Pagninus and Arias have "griffin". So too, among the Hebrews, Pomarius, who holds that Perusia, a town of the Etruscans, took its name from it, and therefore has the פרס peres, or griffin, in its arms. Yet Origen, book 4 Against Celsus, rightly observes that the griffin has never ὑποχείριον ἀνθρώπων γεγονέναι [hypocheirion anthrōpōn gegonenai]. And whatever those most frivolous writers Ctesias and Aristeas of Proconnesus relate about griffins, Pliny, Arrian and Pausanias quite rightly reject as fabulous, as we show elsewhere. This rendering, therefore, cannot stand, unless by the name gryps [griffin] something other than the common meaning is understood, namely γρυπαίετος [grypaietos], that is, an eagle with a remarkably hooked beak. For that is properly γρυπότης [grypotēs]. The beak, of course, usually has the same hookedness as the talons. Further, I think those ancient interpreters conjectured that the name פרס peres signifies a bird with especially large talons because the Hebrew פרסה parsa, "hoof", is written with almost the same letters. But this conjecture pleases me less, because פרסה parsa is only the hoof of quadrupeds, while that of birds is צפרן tsipporen, in Chaldee טפר tephar, Dan. IV, 30.

For the Samaritan, פרס peres is ࠁࠆࠀࠄ bezaa, the hawk; so too for Münster and Schindler. But for Jonathan it is עוזא uza, of which in the next chapter. For the Arabs it is عقاب [ʿuqāb] okab, the melanaeetus. For the Jews in Germany it is בלאבֿוז blafus, as if you were to say "blue-foot". So they call a kind of falcon from its blue feet, of which Albertus says: The ninth kind of falcons, already falling short of the excellence of the noble falcons, is the one [col. 186] [II, 771] whose feet are hyacinthine or azure, etc. By the Italians, according to Gesner, it is called zafiro from the sapphire colour of its feet. Following this, Diodati rendered it "falcon" in his Italian version, and "gerfalcon" in the French. The first origin of this rendering will now be explained. The old French word pers, derived from prasinus [leek-green], first meant a green, then also a blue colour. When the Jews, who once lived in large numbers in France, noticed this, those witless men inferred that the bird פרס peres is at least partly blue in colour, as if our pers for blue were formed from the Hebrew. This is utterly absurd. But raving is customary with those men. And by no less ridiculous an error David de Pomis recently asserted that this very word פרס peres produced the name of Perusia (an old town of the Etruscans, mentioned besides Ptolemy by Silius, Appian, Eutropius, Stephanus and others).

From the same flock, someone cited by Münster decided that the פרס peres is a bird found only in Persia, as if פרס peres alluded to the Hebrew word for Persia, פרס paras. But this conjecture too is empty, for two reasons. 1. Because the name of Persia is about nine hundred years more recent than Moses: it arose in the time of Cyrus, who first taught his countrymen to ride. Hence those who were formerly Cuthaeans, or Cissians, Susians and Elamites began to be called פרסין or פרשין, Persians or horsemen, as we proved in our Phaleg. 2. Because Moses would not have forbidden the Jews a bird peculiar to Persia, which is immensely distant from Judaea. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that a certain bird had its name from Persia, which Aristophanes in the Birds calls Περσικὸν ὄρνιν [Persikon ornin]. But the Scholiast writes that some understand τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα [ton alektryona], others τὸν ταῶ [ton taō], the peacock; both of these birds are clean, whereas the peres is unclean.

Now it is worth knowing why Junius renders פרס, peres, "ossifrage", and Castalio anataria [duck-eagle], which are species of eagles. The verb פרס paras, from which פרס peres comes, first means to divide and to distribute, then also to break, because things are divided by breaking. Castalio had this in view, because Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, writes of the duck-eagle: It has the habit of breaking tortoises it has seized by dropping them from on high, a fate which killed the poet Aeschylus. But Junius, as if פרס peres were named from distributing, gives this reason for his rendering in his Notes: The ossifrage has its name from distributing, because Pliny attributes this to the creature: The related kind, the ossifrages, take in the young cast out by the eagles and rear them with their own. Yet in these words of Pliny there is not even a γρῦ [gry] about distribution, except καθ᾽ ἀκολούθησιν [kath᾽ akolouthēsin]; for since the ossifrage feeds strange young with its own, it must divide the food between both. Nor is the name of the ossifrage from distributing, but from the breaking of bones, as everyone knows.

[II, 772] Having thus set out the opinions of others, we shall here also present our own and try to support it with suitable arguments. First, I side with those who hold that פרס peres is a species of eagle. Among them are the Greeks, Jerome, the Chaldeans, the Arabs and most of the more recent writers. In favour of this is the fact that among the Macedonians, who enriched from the spoils of the East not only their wealth but also their language, the eagle was called παραὸς [paraos], in manifest allusion to the Hebrew פרס peres. Hesychius: Παραός· ἀετὸς ὑπὸ Μακεδόνων· [Paraos; aetos hypo Makedonōn;] Paraos, the eagle among the Macedonians. Moreover, just as by universal agreement נשר denotes the true eagle, so it is very probable that the words immediately following in Moses, namely פרס and עזניה, designate other species of eagles known to the Jews. Nor is it safe to oppose so many interpreters who hold this view. Let it stand firm, then, that פרס is among the species of eagles. But now we must inquire into the species, which can be extracted from nothing else than the origin of the word, since apart from the bare name we have nothing whatever about it. And Aben Ezra rightly [col. 187] notes that the origin is to be taken from these words of Es. LVIII, 7: פרוס לרעב לחמך Break your bread for the hungry. By this note he meant to indicate that it is a kind of eagle so called from breaking. But to make the matter clearer, consider, reader, these words of Mich. III, 3., which it is surprising have not yet been cited in this discussion: ואת עצמותיהם פצחו ופרשו כאשר בסיר וכבשר בתוך קלחת, And they broke their bones and shattered them as in a pot, and as flesh in the midst of a cauldron. From this it is evident that the verb פרס (or פרש with Sin Semol, which is the same) is also used of the breaking of bones. From this, then, there is no one who would not conclude that פרס peres is the ossifrage, that is, that species of eagle which from breaking bones is called in the Roman tongue ossifraga or ossifragus [bone-breaker], and in Arabic either simply كاسر [kāsir], that is, breaker, or كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones ^{(1)}. Thus Junius rightly rendered it ossifrage, although the true reason for this rendering escaped him. And perhaps it bears on the same point that for פרס Onkelos and the Jerusalem Targum have ער or עריא. For the words ער and עריא, with the radicals inverted, could have been derived from the verbs רעע or רעה, which mean to break and to crush. Of the ossifrage Lucretius writes thus, book 5, line 1077:
Lastly the race of winged things, and the various birds, hawks and ossifrages — — —

And Pliny uses it throughout, as in book 10, ch. 3, where he speaks of the haliaeetus: That which is born from them has its kind among the ossifrages. And a little later: Some add a kind of eagle which they call the bearded eagle; the Tuscans, however, call it the ossifrage. And again, where he speaks of the chicks [II, 773] that eagles throw out because they are weary of feeding them: When they have been thrown out by these, the related kind of the ossifrage takes them up and rears them with its own. And in ch. 7: Some think that the immussulus is the chick of the vulture, and the sanqualis that of the ossifrage. Likewise Massurius says that the sanqualis is the ossifrage. And in book 30, ch. 7: The ossifrage has a single intestine of wonderful nature, which digests everything it has swallowed. And a little before: The stomach of the ossifrage, dried and taken in drink, is very useful to those who do not digest their food. And in the chapter immediately following he prescribes that the same be taken to expel stones. Isidore too, book 12, ch. 7: The bird that drops bones from on high and breaks them is commonly called ossifrangus (read ossifragus), and hence it received its name from breaking bones. See also Festus under the words immussulus and sanqualis. Ossifragus is rendered in Greek in one Glossary as ὀστοκόπος [ostokopos], ὀστοκλάστης [ostoklastēs], ὀστοκατεάκτης [ostokateaktēs]; in another, but wrongly, as ὀστοκόραξ [ostokorax]; in Dioscorides as φίνις [phinis]. Φίνις [Phinis], he says, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον [to orneon, ho Rhōmaisti kalousin ossiphragon]. And among older writers it is φήνη [phēnē], a word very well known from Homer and Aristotle, and one which the Arabs also use. Damir, from Ibnosaida: الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فاذا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن [al-fīna ṭāyir yushbih al-ʿuqāb fa-idhā khāfa al-bard inḥadara ilā al-Yaman] Phena, a bird resembling the eagle, which, when it fears the cold, goes off to Ieman, that is, to Arabia Felix. But it is commonly called, as we have said, كاسر [kāsir] breaker, and كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones. Also مكلفة [mukallafa] mechalapha, from its black colour mixed with reddish or yellowish. Damir: الكاسر العقاب [al-kāsir al-ʿuqāb] Alchasir (or breaker) is a kind of eagle. The same elsewhere: كاسر العظام المكلفة [kāsir al-ʿiẓām al-mukallafa] The breaker of bones, that is, the mechalepha. And in the chapter On the mechalepha: الفرخ الذي ترمي [col. 188] به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه [al-farkh alladhī tarmī bihi al-ʿuqāb min al-thalatha yaḥḍunuhu ṭāyir yuqāl lahu al-mukallafa wa-yuqāl lahu kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-turabbīhi] The chick which the eagle has thrown out of the three is warmed and fed by a bird which is called mechalepha and breaker of bones. And in the chapter العقاب [al-ʿuqāb], or On the eagle: والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر [wa-al-ʿarab yusammī al-ʿuqāb al-kāsir] The Arabs also call the eagle (that is, a species of eagle) the breaker. And below: والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه [wa-al-farkh alladhī tulqīhi yaʿṭifu ʿalayhi ṭāyir yusammā kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-yusammā al-mukallafa ayḍan fa-yurabbīhi] And on the chick thrown out by the eagle a bird takes pity, which is named ossifrage and mechalepha, so that it rears it. It is evident that the French orfraye is derived from ossifraga, although among us it denotes something else, namely the haliaeetus or sea eagle. This was observed long ago by Belon, On Birds, book 2, ch. 7.
